explanations.answer: Confront her with all her abominations
explanations.explanation: That's the job, friend. God tells Ezekiel, the prophet He's speaking to, to confront the city of bloodshed with all her abominations (Ezekiel 22:2). It's not a job anybody puts on a vision board. I think I'd have asked if there was a smaller assignment, like sweeping the bakery.

explanations.answer: Comfort her in all her troubles
explanations.explanation: Comfort is a lovely idea, baker, but it's not what God asks for here. He tells Ezekiel, the prophet, to confront her with all her abominations (Ezekiel 22:2). The word is aimed straight at what she's been doing. This is the kind of moment where you set the cookie tray down and listen.

explanations.answer: Remind her of all her victories
explanations.explanation: No victory lap in this one, friend. God never mentions her wins. He says to confront her with all her abominations (Ezekiel 22:2). Ezekiel, the prophet, is handed a hard message, not a trophy shelf.

Idols, baker. God says the city brings her own doom by shedding blood within her walls and making idols to defile herself (Ezekiel 22:3). Two things are named, and the blood comes first. Verse 4 says she's guilty of the blood and defiled by the idols she made.

Treaties never come up in this verse, friend. God names the blood shed within her walls and the idols she made to defile herself (Ezekiel 22:3). Nobody here is signing paperwork. The word that fits the blank is idols.
I see why you went there, since blood is in the same sentence. But the verse doesn't say weapons. God says she makes idols to defile herself (Ezekiel 22:3). The blank is idols, baker.

Right, and God says it plainly: “Those near and far will mock you, O infamous city, full of turmoil.” (Ezekiel 22:5) Verse 4 says He has made her a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the lands. Near and far both get a say. I know a little about being the punchline myself, friend.

Nobody's coming with a rope, baker. God says those near and far will mock her (Ezekiel 22:5). He has made her a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the lands (Ezekiel 22:4). Mockery is what the text gives, and it doesn't mention rescue.

Fear would be a respectable reaction, but it's not the one in the text. God says those near and far will mock her (Ezekiel 22:5). A mockery to all the lands, that's how verse 4 puts it. Fear isn't what the verse gives, friend.

I know it sounds like the right thing to say, but the text says the opposite. God says, “Father and mother are treated with contempt.” (Ezekiel 22:7) Honor isn't the word the verse uses. Contempt is, baker.
False it is, friend. God says, “Father and mother are treated with contempt.” (Ezekiel 22:7) Contempt, not honor. It's one line in a long list of what's happening inside her walls.

That's it, baker. God says, “…the foreign resident is exploited, the fatherless and the widow are oppressed.” (Ezekiel 22:7) Three groups are named in that one verse. I think this one hits hard, and it's worth slowing down for.

Not here, friend. In this verse the ones oppressed are the fatherless and the widow, along with the foreign resident (Ezekiel 22:7). The priests aren't listed as the oppressed ones. Those three are the ones named.

Switched sides on that one, baker. The princes are named in verse 6 as the ones who have used their power to shed blood (Ezekiel 22:6). The people oppressed in verse 7 are the fatherless and the widow, along with the foreign resident (Ezekiel 22:7).
Profaned, baker. God says, “You have despised My holy things and profaned My Sabbaths.” (Ezekiel 22:8) Holy things got treated like common ones. Two charges in one sentence, and they go together.
If only, friend. Honoring would be the opposite of what God says here. He says, “You have despised My holy things and profaned My Sabbaths.” (Ezekiel 22:8) The blank is profaned.
Guarding isn't in the verse, baker. God says she despised His holy things and profaned His Sabbaths (Ezekiel 22:8). The word in the blank is profaned.

Forgotten, friend. After the bribes and the extortion, God says, “But Me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 22:12) The city is the one who forgot, not God. I know a thing or two about being left in the back of a drawer, and this one hits me too.

Fear is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the word here. God says, “But Me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 22:12) That comes right after the bribes to shed blood and the extorting of neighbors. The word in the blank is forgotten.
Sought is a good word, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. God says, “But Me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 22:12) The blank is forgotten.
True, baker. God says, “I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act.” (Ezekiel 22:14) He's not hinting and He's not guessing. When He says it, He means it.

That one's true, friend, even if it's a heavy line. God says, “I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act.” (Ezekiel 22:14) He tells the city He has spoken, and He says He will act. No hedging in that sentence.

That's what He says, baker. “I will disperse you among the nations and scatter you throughout the lands; I will purge your uncleanness.” (Ezekiel 22:15) Dispersed and scattered, and both words are there. It's a heavy word, so I'll just let it sit.

explanations.answer: Hide them up in the mountains
explanations.explanation: No mountain hideout in this verse, friend. The mountain shrines in verse 9 are where some people were eating, and that's a different thing (Ezekiel 22:9). God says He will disperse them among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands (Ezekiel 22:15).

explanations.answer: Send them all back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't mentioned in this passage, baker. God says, “I will disperse you among the nations and scatter you throughout the lands…” (Ezekiel 22:15). Scattered among the nations, not sent back to one place. Good guess though, since you were thinking about other lands.

Yes, friend. God says that when she has defiled herself in the eyes of the nations, she will know that He is the LORD (Ezekiel 22:16). It's a phrase that shows up again in this chapter, in verse 22. She forgot Him, and she'll know Him.
The idols don't get a victory lap here, baker. God says she will know that He is the LORD (Ezekiel 22:16). Nothing in the verse says her idols are strong. The idols are what defiled her in verse 3.
Not the princes, friend. The princes were the ones using their power to shed blood (Ezekiel 22:6). What God says she'll know is that He is the LORD (Ezekiel 22:16).

Jerusalem, baker. God says, “Because all of you have become dross, behold, I will gather you into Jerusalem.” (Ezekiel 22:19) The furnace picture comes next. Dross is the leftover scum that gets skimmed off when metal is melted.

Babylon isn't named in this passage, friend. God says, “…I will gather you into Jerusalem.” (Ezekiel 22:19) The gathering happens in Jerusalem, and the melting happens within the city. Keep your eyes on that city name.
Samaria doesn't come up in these verses, baker. God says, “…I will gather you into Jerusalem.” (Ezekiel 22:19) That's the city He names. The furnace picture comes right after it in the passage.

True, friend. God says, “…I will gather you in My anger and wrath, leave you there, and melt you.” (Ezekiel 22:20) The furnace picture is clear, with the gathering first and the melting after. It's a heavy word, and I won't make it lighter than it is.

It's a hard line, baker, but it's true. God says, “…I will gather you in My anger and wrath, leave you there, and melt you.” (Ezekiel 22:20) He gathers them first, then leaves them there. Then comes the melting.

Cleansed, baker. God says, “In the day of indignation, you are a land that has not been cleansed, upon which no rain has fallen.” (Ezekiel 22:24) That's the word that fills the blank. He's speaking about the day of indignation.
Conquering is a different word, friend. The verse says, “…you are a land that has not been cleansed, upon which no rain has fallen.” (Ezekiel 22:24) Conquered isn't in it. The blank is cleansed.
Nobody's taking a census here, baker. God says the land has not been cleansed, and no rain has fallen on it (Ezekiel 22:24). Think of a dusty counter that nobody has wiped. The blank is cleansed.

The widows, friend. God says the princes “…devour the people, seize the treasures and precious things, and multiply the widows within her.” (Ezekiel 22:25) That's a sober line. I think it's one to hold quietly.

Harvests would be good news, baker, and this isn't good news. God says the princes “…devour the people, seize the treasures and precious things, and multiply the widows within her.” (Ezekiel 22:25) What they multiply is the widows.

Soldiers don't show up in this verse, friend. God says the princes devour the people, seize the treasures and precious things, and multiply the widows within her (Ezekiel 22:25). The answer is the widows.

Common, baker. God says the priests “…make no distinction between the holy and the common, and they fail to distinguish between the clean and the unclean.” (Ezekiel 22:26) The people who should know the difference don't draw the line. They also disregard His Sabbaths.

Ancient is a fine word, friend, but it's not in this sentence. God says the priests make no distinction between the holy and the common (Ezekiel 22:26). The line they should be drawing is between holy and common. The blank is common.

Foreign came up earlier, in the foreign resident in verse 7, and it's easy to carry over (Ezekiel 22:7). But here God says the priests make no distinction between the holy and the common (Ezekiel 22:26). The blank is common, baker.

Whitewash, baker. God says, “Her prophets whitewash these deeds by false visions and lying divinations…” (Ezekiel 22:28). It's like painting over a crack in the wall and calling the house fine. The crack is still there.
That's not what the verse says, friend. God says they whitewash the deeds by false visions and lying divinations (Ezekiel 22:28). The verse says whitewash, not expose.

explanations.answer: Hide away from them in the hills
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about hiding in the hills, baker. God says the prophets whitewash these deeds by false visions and lying divinations (Ezekiel 22:28). The word for what they do with the deeds is whitewash.

I wish that were the case, friend, but the text says the opposite. God says, “The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have oppressed the poor and needy…” (Ezekiel 22:29). The everyday people aren't off the hook here. They have also exploited the foreign resident without justice.

False, baker. God says, “The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have oppressed the poor and needy and have exploited the foreign resident without justice.” (Ezekiel 22:29) It isn't only the leaders. The whole land is in this.

No one, baker. God says, “I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one.” (Ezekiel 22:30) I think this is the heaviest line in the chapter. It deserves a quiet moment.
I wish it said that, friend. But God says, “But I found no one.” (Ezekiel 22:30) He searched for a man to repair the wall and stand in the gap. The answer is no one, and I think that's a sad one.

Even a handful would have been something, baker, but the text says otherwise. God says He searched for a man to stand in the gap on behalf of the land, and then says, “But I found no one.” (Ezekiel 22:30) I think this one hurts.
